band.text:
The tea is free to volunteers and a pound to visitors, the biscuits are whatever the last person
brought, and the kettle is the only appliance in the cottage that is never switched off at the wall. The
mugs are washed by whoever drinks from them. This is written down because it was once not, and
the resulting week was long.

The observatory closes for the first two weeks of January, when the cottage is cleaned, the hides are
repaired, the store is emptied and dried, and the log is bound and shelved. The census is walked
even then, by the warden, because forty years without a gap is a thing worth keeping.

provenance.key:
The boat is the observatory's only vehicle, an aluminium dinghy on a trailer behind the store, and it
goes out only with the warden, only on a neap tide, and only to reach the spit when the boardwalk
is under water after a surge. It is not a pleasure boat and is not lent; the lifejackets hang beside it
and are worn, and the outboard is run for ten minutes on the first Saturday of the month whether it
is needed or not.

The committee meets in February, June and October in the cottage, and the minutes are pinned on
the wall for a month and then filed. Anything that changes these notes is decided there and
nowhere else, and a volunteer who thinks a rule is wrong is asked to bring it to the meeting rather
than to stop keeping it.

Lastly, these notes are revised every February by the warden and each version is dated and kept on
the shelf with the reports. Most of the rules here were paid for by a lost net, a flooded store, a
frightened visitor or a bird that should not have died, and the notes are shorter than that list.
